country.comment: National water policy analysis of Morocco (1995-2020) combined with primary qualitative fieldwork in the Middle Draa Valley (south Morocco).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 2

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative policy content analysis and interview/focus-group case study; no statistical point estimates, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported (descriptive interview perceptions such as 70% vs. 30% irrigating during a dam release are anecdotal interviewee remarks rather than study-estimated statistical effects).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Content analysis of 10 policy documents and fieldwork in the Middle Draa Valley show that Morocco's 1995-2020 water policy prioritizes engineering supply expansion and economic efficiency while neglecting institutional, social, and political determinants of water access and failing to prevent aquifer depletion: (1) potable water shortages and service intermittency persist, with some households still lacking piped drinking-water connections; (2) surface irrigation access is unequally mediated by uneven customary water rights and turn orders, canal distance, and upstream-downstream power asymmetries in WUA dam-release scheduling; (3) drip-irrigation subsidies exclude smallholder oasis farmers with fragmented plots (<5 ha) because private installers refuse small surfaces, while accelerating groundwater-intensive agriculture on collective lands outside oases; and (4) compartmentalization across the Ministries of Agriculture, Water, and Interior, omission of well-digging permit checks in drip-irrigation subsidy applications, contradictory tribal land-use certificate and well-permitting rules, and weak regulatory enforcement incentivize unauthorized well digging and intensify groundwater depletion and conflict with municipal drinking-water supply.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 13-19, Section 3.2; PDF pp. 19-22, Sections 4-5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative case study appraised with CASP (design ceiling = 2). Through interviews with government officials, WUA representatives, and local inhabitants/farmers plus policy document analysis, the study directly documents how administrative compartmentalization, subsidy eligibility procedures, contradictory tribal land-use and state well-permitting rules, customary water rights, and non-enforcement shape unequal water access and unauthorized groundwater extraction.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 4-5, Section 2; PDF pp. 13-19, Section 3.2

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines customary water shares/rights and collective tribal land tenure (ELIGIBILITY, property, tenure); contractor requirements for drip-irrigation subsidies and circular procedural contradictions between tribal land-use certificates and state well-digging permits, alongside omission of digging-permit verification in subsidy applications (BURDEN, documentation, procedural_steps); administrative forbearance/discretion and informal influence/bribes in groundwater regulation, plus WUA participatory scheduling and severe inter-ministerial compartmentalization across Agriculture, Water, and Interior (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, discretion, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination); and lack of regulatory enforcement/sanctions against illegal well drilling (ENFORCEMENT, sanction).
